<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-grounded cases without fake citations, and the debate stayed sharply on the proposition. But CON landed the more damaging and ultimately unanswered blow: in Rebuttal 2 (A4.1-A4.2), CON pointed out that PRO's model gives the verification team the right to "publicly confirm findings even over host objection" regardless of whether the government is honestly overwhelmed or deliberately concealing — meaning even a cooperative ministry that opens the door still loses control of the narrative the instant the team speaks. This directly undercut PRO's central pressure-question answer that "opening the door proves you're overwhelmed and pulls help in, not punishment." PRO's closing reasserted the general "leaks happen anyway" and "refusal starts a clock" lines but never squarely rebutted the specific claim that honest cooperation itself is punished under PRO's own proposed rule, leaving that route live at the end of the debate. CON's answers to PRO's pressure questions (A4.1, A4.3) were more incisive than PRO's answers to CON's questions (B4.1, B4.3), the latter relying on a somewhat asserted claim that markets/airlines would costlessly punish even great powers, without engaging CON's earlier point that WHO enforcement is inherently asymmetric. CON's closing crystallized this into a clean, memorable frame ("what does a government do the moment it learns this rule exists") that PRO's closing did not fully neutralize.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 point (A4.1-A4.2) that PRO's "publish over host objection" mechanism punishes honest, overwhelmed ministries identically to deliberate concealers — a critique PRO's closing never directly answered.</best_rebuttal>
